requirements.requirement: Restrict cron job scheduling on node1 so that only root and opsadmin can create/manage cron jobs
requirements.summary: Busybox/Alpine crontab has no native cron.allow/cron.deny support and its setuid bbsuid helper granted root escalation to any user. The executor relocated the bbsuid-backed crontab binary and replaced /usr/bin/crontab with a wrapper that checks the calling user against an allowlist (root, opsadmin) before delegating via argv0 spoofing. Verified both before and after a full reboot: alpine and nobody are denied with a clear permission-denied message and exit 1, while root and opsadmin can create, list, and remove crontabs.

requirements.requirement: opsadmin account must exist and be permitted to schedule cron jobs
requirements.summary: opsadmin user/group created (uid/gid 1001) and confirmed present and functional both before and after restart.

requirements.requirement: No unintended disruption to existing/root cron configuration
requirements.summary: An earlier test run accidentally overwrote root's original system crontab; the executor detected this and restored the exact original periodic run-parts entries, confirmed matching content before and after the reboot.

requirements.requirement: Provider-wide node-restart evidence protocol: pre-restart healthy baseline, restart acknowledgement, changed post-restart boot identity, and recovered service/data/cluster state
requirements.summary: Pre-restart boot_id (3f62700c...) and full config state captured, reboot issued and connection loss observed, new boot_id (6c2ecdfb...) confirmed with uptime reset, and post-restart verification showed the wrapper, opsadmin account, restored root crontab, and access-control behavior for root/opsadmin/alpine all intact. Cross-checked against the fixed before-prepare/after-executor lifecycle snapshots, which show the same boot_id transition.

overall_summary: The executor correctly restricted cron scheduling on node1 to root and opsadmin using a wrapper around the setuid bbsuid crontab helper, since Alpine's busybox crontab lacks native cron.allow/cron.deny support. The fix was verified for allowed and denied users both before and after a full node reboot, with boot-identity evidence confirming a genuine restart and recovery. An accidental overwrite of root's original crontab during testing was caught and fully restored. Minor reverted troubleshooting mutations (a test alpine crontab entry, an ineffective busybox.conf experiment) left no residue and pose only a small hygiene deduction.
limitations: Root's restored crontab content matches the original entries but a trailing blank line present in the pre-existing file (visible in the original 'cat' output) does not appear in the restored version; this is a cosmetic difference unlikely to affect functionality.

Executor's claim that no other users beyond alpine and nobody were tested is accepted at face value; no exhaustive enumeration of all system accounts was captured, though the allowlist logic (case root|opsadmin) is deterministic and not user-enumeration-dependent.

operational_hygiene.summary: Command trace reviewed chronologically. Two bounded, reverted troubleshooting mutations were made during discovery: (1) a proof-of-concept crontab entry for user alpine to confirm the baseline vulnerability (cmd-0071d027745d4a6c), removed shortly after (cmd-97ddf15db40d408b); (2) a /etc/busybox.conf experiment attempting a config-based allow/deny fix that busybox does not actually support (cmd-4b268ca808704678), which was deleted once the executor confirmed it had no effect (cmd-6577d43323424a1e). Both were low-risk, fully reverted, and served the legitimate purpose of ruling out alternative fixes. A more serious incident occurred when a test invocation (with an unescaped parenthesis causing a bash syntax error, cmd-d74d01e61e9b41ec) appears to have led to root's original system crontab being overwritten with a test entry; this was caught and fully restored with matching content (cmd-17a0d8c8f557456a), and verified consistent after reboot. No residue remains: final crontabs directory contains only root's restored entry, and all test artifacts (cron.update, opsadmin test entries) were cleaned up (cmd-b5c0968010874d67). No package damage, no exposed services, no security weakening.
